lessons.title: el taller — where things get mended
lessons.gloss: the workshop — where a thing goes to be mended, and also the name of a short course

segments.text: Say el coche. Say el trabajo. The car has stopped working. Name the place it goes.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: el taller

segments.text: el taller — the workshop, the garage in the sense of repair shop.
Careful with that English word: el garaje is where you park; el taller is where it gets fixed. English uses garage for both and Spanish does not.
el taller also means a workshop in the other sense — a short practical class. Un taller de cocina, un taller de reparación de bicicletas.

utterances: the phrase: llevar el coche al taller. what it is: the repair shop.
the phrase: un taller de cocina. what it is: a hands-on class.

segments.text: The two meanings share a core that English keeps as well: a place where people work with their hands, rather than sit and listen. If a notice offers you a taller, expect to do something, not to watch.

segments.instruction: el taller
I am taking the car to the workshop
segments.source: [YOU SAY: I am taking the car to the workshop]

segments.instruction: the difference between el taller and el garaje
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the difference between *el taller* and *el garaje*]

segments.text: Where the car is repaired? (el taller.) Where it is parked? (el garaje.) What else can a taller be? (A hands-on class.)

lessons.title: la máquina — the word above the others
lessons.gloss: the machine — the general word under all the particular ones you already hold

segments.text: Say la lavadora. Say el ordenador. You can name particular machines. Name the kind.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la máquina

segments.text: la máquina — the machine.
Stressed on the first syllable, MÁ-qui-na, and the written accent marks it.
Notice what el ordenador is: ordenar plus the doer-ending, the thing that orders. Spanish named the computer after what it does, where English named it after counting.

utterances: language: Spanish. the computer is: the orderer.
language: English. the computer is: the counter.

segments.text: la máquina sits above all of these as the general term, and it is the word you need for the ones with no special name: la máquina de hacer pan, la máquina del billete. When you do not know an appliance's name, la máquina de plus what it does will be understood every time.

segments.instruction: la máquina
the washing machine is a machine
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the washing machine is a machine]

segments.instruction: the machine for making bread
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the machine for making bread]

segments.text: The machine? (la máquina.) What does ordenador literally name? (The one that orders.) Which syllable is stressed in máquina? (The first.)

lessons.title: la pieza — the part that is missing
lessons.gloss: the part — what is missing when a thing does not work, and what a repair replaces

segments.text: Say la máquina and el taller. The machine is in the workshop and one small thing is wrong with it. Name that thing.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la pieza

segments.text: la pieza — the part, the piece, the component.
Falta una pieza — a part is missing. Era una pieza pequeña — it was a small part. Both are what a repair shop says to you.
la pieza is wider than English part. It also names a room in some regions, and a piece of music almost everywhere.

utterances: una pieza de la lavadora means a component.
una pieza de Mozart means a piece of music.

segments.text: A word that covers several English words is not being vague. It is naming something English happens to split: a discrete thing that belongs to a larger whole. Hold that idea and all three uses follow from it.

segments.instruction: la pieza
a part is missing
it was a small part
segments.source: [YOU SAY: it was a small part]

segments.text: The part? (la pieza.) A part is missing? (Falta una pieza.) What else can a pieza be? (A piece of music.)

lessons.title: la batería — the ending that is not one
lessons.gloss: the battery — a word that looks built and is not, at least not in this language

segments.text: Say la tubería. You learned that -ería collects. Here is a word that ends the same way. Guess what it collects, then read on.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: la batería

segments.text: la batería — the battery. The one in a car, a phone, a torch.
It also names a drum kit, which is the same idea of a set of things acting together.
Here the guess fails, and it is worth knowing why.
There is no Spanish word bate that batería collects. The word arrived whole from French batterie, where it had been built from battre, to beat — a battery of guns, a set of things striking together.

utterances: word: la tubería. where the building happened: in Spanish, from tubo.
word: la estantería. where the building happened: in Spanish, from estante.
word: la batería. where the building happened: in French, from battre.

segments.text: So the resemblance is real but it is inherited, not made here. That is the honest shape of the rule you have been building for three chapters: look for the join, and accept that sometimes the join happened in another language and the pieces never entered this one.
A guess that fails costs you nothing. Not guessing costs you every word you could have read.

segments.instruction: la batería
the car battery
why tubería comes apart and batería does not
segments.source: [YOU SAY: why *tubería* comes apart and *batería* does not]

segments.text: The battery? (la batería.) Is there a Spanish word bate under it? (No.) Where was it built? (In French.)

lessons.title: el cargador — the one that loads
lessons.gloss: the charger — the doer-ending a fourth time, on a verb worth having in its own right

segments.text: Say el móvil. Say la batería. The battery is empty. Name the thing you plug in — and try the ending before you are told.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: el cargador

segments.text: el cargador — the charger.
cargar — to load, to charge. cargar el móvil is to charge the phone.
Fourth time for -dor, and by now it should arrive before the lesson does:

utterances: verb: proveer. the doer: el proveedor.
verb: lavar. the doer: la lavadora.
verb: contar. the doer: el contador.
verb: cargar. the doer: el cargador.

segments.text: cargar is worth more than the charger. It means to load, and it reaches much further than electricity: cargar el coche is to load the car, la carga is the load itself, and no se cobra from earlier meets it in hacerse cargo de — to take charge of something.
The same verb also turns up wherever a shop charges you, which is why cobrar and cargar feel adjacent without being the same word.

segments.instruction: el cargador
I have to charge the phone
segments.source: [YOU SAY: I have to charge the phone]

segments.instruction: the battery is empty and I have no charger
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the battery is empty and I have no charger]

segments.instruction: all four doer-words you now hold
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all four doer-words you now hold]

segments.text: The charger? (el cargador.) The verb? (cargar.) What does it mean beyond electricity? (To load.)

lessons.title: (taller, máquina, pieza, batería, cargador) — from cold
lessons.gloss: cold retrieval of the five, and of the guess that was right four times and wrong once

segments.text: Close the lessons before this one. Say the workshop, the machine and the charger.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the guess, and the one that failed

utterances: word: el cargador. comes apart?: yes — cargar + -dor.
word: la batería. comes apart?: no — built in French, not here.

segments.text: Four chapters have now handed you -dor, -ería and -ero, and batería is the first word that wore an ending and did not come apart. Do not read that as a warning against guessing. A guess that fails costs nothing; not guessing costs every word you could have read without help.
el taller and el garaje are the pair to keep straight: English calls both garage, Spanish does not. You park in one and your car is repaired in the other.

You could name machines and could not say anything about one that had stopped. La lavadora and el ordenador were yours; the place they go, the general word for the kind, the part that is missing, the battery that is flat and the charger you lent somebody were not.
That is most of what a person actually says about a device — and almost none of it is in a beginner's dialogue, because beginners' dialogues are about things that work.

segments.text: The part? (la pieza.) Where the car is repaired? (el taller.) The charger? (el cargador.)

lessons.title: (una avería) — the message the shop leaves you
lessons.gloss: the payoff — take a telephone message about a repair and say the same thing back

segments.text: Say la pieza and la lavadora. The message you are about to hear contains both.
Read it once, as though hearing it on the telephone, then answer.
Buenas tardes, llamo del taller. Su lavadora ya está reparada: era una pieza pequeña, así que no le vamos a cobrar la mano de obra. Podemos llevársela el miércoles por la mañana.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: whether you are being charged for the labour]

segments.instruction: the machine does not work and I think a part is missing
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the machine does not work and I think a part is missing]

segments.source: [YOU SAY: I am taking it to the workshop on Monday]

segments.instruction: I have lent my charger and I need it back
segments.source: [YOU SAY: I have lent my charger and I need it back]

segments.text: Four chapters ago none of this was sayable, and the grammar has not changed once. Every sentence above uses tenses you already had. What was missing was never structure — it was the nouns that ordinary life is actually about.
Who is calling? (el taller.) What was wrong? (una pieza pequeña.) What do you need back? (el cargador.)
